name: Coffee shop
tagline: Espresso, pastries and 18 seats on a real New York block: real rent, real permits, real inspectors.

unit.name: order
unit.note: Planning assumption from research notes (economics.md, 2026 planning model): an average ticket of $8.50 before sales tax (a drink, sometimes with a pastry). Menu anchors seen by the note's author in 2026: latte $4.25-$6.99, croissant $4.00-$5.49. Ingredients, food and spoilage are 26% of sales = $2.21 per order; cups, lids and napkins (another 2%) are a separate monthly cost line, so the full cost of goods is 28%. No public statistic of the average NYC cafe ticket exists.

market.note: Planning assumption from research notes (economics.md, 2026 planning model): 200 orders a day x 30 days = 6,000 a month for one average storefront at $8.50 and average quality. The notes stress that this is a scenario, not a measured "typical" figure: count foot traffic yourself. Elasticity and weights are game-balance values kept from the engine fixture.

capacity.note: Four baristas at 160 paid hours each serve the reference 6,000 orders with about 12% slack: 1,700 orders per person a month, roughly 10.6 orders per paid hour. Planning assumption from the research notes (four baristas for 200 orders a day over a 12-hour day, with the owner or a hired manager as a fifth pair of hands). Two people is the legal and practical floor: someone holding a Food Protection Certificate must be on site every open hour.

sizing.note: My estimates, sized to the research notes' shop (about 800 sq ft, 15-25 seats, 20 chairs at 10 small tables). 18 sq ft per seat with aisles: 800 sq ft x 60% usable / 18 = 26 seats at most. 60% of orders leave with the cup. One seat turns about 5.7 sit-down orders a day (170 a month), so 18 seats carry 255 orders a day in all and 12 seats only 170: at 200 orders a day the small room turns people away, while 40 seats sit two-thirds empty: a room less than 40% used reads as dead and costs reputation. $15 per seat a month covers sanitizer, paper goods, table and floor care. Real rule seen at NYC Health: 20 or more seats, indoor plus outdoor, require a customer bathroom.

setup.name: Lease security deposit (three months of rent)
setup.note: Three months of this address's rent: the reserve chosen in the research notes (the fallback $18,000 is 3 x $6,000). Seen in the NYC Commercial Lease Guide: the deposit is commonly two months of rent but depends on the tenant's finances, and a new business may be asked for much more or for a personal guaranty. Refundable at the end of the lease.

setup.name: Build-out: what it takes to turn this space into a cafe
setup.note: Priced by what the space was before, per square foot of this address (extra.buildout). Research notes, 2026: a former cafe that keeps its plumbing, ventilation and bathroom $87.50 per sq ft; a former restaurant or food shop $225 per sq ft (the contractor's 2026 guide gives $200-$300 for a counter-service cafe in a former food space); a space that never had food service $400 per sq ft (the guide gives $400-$600 or more). The fallback $70,000 is the former cafe at 800 sq ft. Covers the counter, finishes, electrical and plumbing hookups; movable equipment is bought separately.

setup.name: Architect, engineer and permit expediter
setup.note: 10% of the build-out: the share chosen in the research notes for filed plans, engineering and a permit expediter (the percentage is the notes' own, not a published tariff). The fallback $7,000 is 10% of a $70,000 light renovation.

setup.name: Lawyer for the lease and contracts
setup.note: Research notes estimate, not a published fee. NYC Small Business Services offers free commercial lease review and legal advice (seen on the NYC Business restaurant page).

setup.name: LLC filing and newspaper publication
setup.note: $200 Articles of Organization (NYS Department of State) + $1,475 all-in publication package for Kings County (Brooklyn), which includes the $50 Certificate of Publication (LLC Publishers price list: Manhattan $1,795, Queens $1,195). Both numbers seen; the package price is one provider's, not a state fee.

setup.name: Two-group espresso machine
setup.note: Nuova Simonelli Appia Life Compact two-group volumetric, 110V: $7,600.00 at WebstaurantStore, usually ships in 2-4 weeks. Price before sales tax, delivery and installation. Lifespan is my estimate.

setup.name: Espresso grinder
setup.note: Mahlkonig E65S grind-by-time: $2,099 at Visions Espresso (listed as discontinued and out of stock on the day I looked; its successor E65W is $3,099). Lifespan is my estimate.

setup.name: Water filtration for the espresso machine
setup.note: Research notes allowance for a filter head, cartridge and fittings; listed there: Everpure ESO7 cartridge $192.94, QL2 head $41.94. Cartridges are replaced several times a year (in the maintenance line).

setup.name: Under-counter milk fridge and reach-in refrigerator
setup.note: Avantco A-19R-HC 29-inch reach-in refrigerator $1,199.00 (seen at WebstaurantStore) + Atosa MGF8401GR under-counter refrigerator $1,429 (from research notes; the dealer page refused my request). Lifespan is my estimate.

setup.name: Refrigerated pastry display case
setup.note: Avantco BCS-48-HC 48-inch refrigerated countertop bakery case: $1,149.00 at WebstaurantStore. Larger floor cases run to $9,800. Lifespan is my estimate.

setup.name: Three-compartment sink, hand sink, mop sink and faucets
setup.note: Research notes basket: three-compartment sink $850 (allowance), hand-wash sink $90, mop sink $280, faucets and fittings $500. Plumbing labor is in the build-out. The Health Code requires a hand-washing sink near every place food is prepared and in each restroom (seen at NYC Health).

setup.name: Stainless prep table and shelving
setup.note: Research notes allowance; needs a real list of sizes.

setup.name: POS register, receipt printer and cash drawer
setup.note: Research notes: Square Register $899 (Square's store, 2026) plus $400 allowance for a printer, cash drawer and mounts. The price was not readable on the page when I opened it.

setup.name: Smallwares: pitchers, tampers, scales, cups, plates, bins
setup.note: Research notes allowance for scales, tampers, pitchers, knock box, thermometers, cups, plates, utensils and food bins.

setup.name: Lidded bins, fire extinguisher, CPR kit, safety signs, alarm
setup.note: Research notes allowance. Seen on the NYC Business restaurant page: restaurants must keep one adult and one pediatric resuscitation mask and two pairs of gloves.

setup.name: Sales tax on equipment, delivery and installation
setup.note: Research notes, "almost ready" column: 8.875% sales tax on about $25,000 of equipment ($2,200) plus freight, unloading and commissioning. Equipment is not bought tax-free: a resale certificate covers only goods you resell.

setup.name: Cafe chair
setup.note: Lancaster Table & Seating metal cafe chairs at WebstaurantStore: $48.99 to $56.49 each; a wood ladder-back chair is $82.49. The research notes used a $39.99 basic chair. One chair per seat.

setup.name: Two-top table (share per seat)
setup.note: Lancaster Table & Seating 24 x 24 inch laminated table top with cast iron base: $69.99 at WebstaurantStore; one table for every two seats = $35 per seat. The research notes budgeted $150 per table set.

setup.name: Opening inventory: beans, milk, syrups, pastries, cups
setup.note: Research notes, "almost ready" column: $3,000 (their fuller basket is $5,000: beans $1,000, tea and syrups $600, milk and first food delivery $900, cups and lids $1,200, cleaning chemicals $500, test drinks and waste $800). Seen: 12 oz hot cups $45.99 per 1,000 at WebstaurantStore. Do not stock milk or pastry for more than a few days.

setup.name: Hiring and paid training before opening
setup.note: Research notes: recruiting plus paid training hours and a soft opening for four baristas (about 190 paid hours at $21). Training time must be paid.

setup.name: First insurance premiums and utility deposits
setup.note: Research notes: first premiums, utility and security deposits, hookups. Seen at Insureon: a business owner's policy for a coffee shop averages $126 a month and workers' comp $88 a month across the US.

setup.name: Food Service Establishment Permit
setup.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
setup.note: NYC Business: the permit fee is $280.00 a year; you can open 22 days after you submit the application even if no pre-permit inspection has taken place. The application asks for proof of workers' compensation and disability insurance, a Food Protection Certificate or course registration, and the sales tax Certificate of Authority. The clock starts when the build-out is finished: the Health Department checks the finished room. The permit does not pass to a buyer of an operating business: the new owner applies again.

setup.name: Food Protection Certificate (course and exam)
setup.note: NYC Health: the online course is free and has 15 lessons; the in-person final exam costs $24. A certified supervisor must be on site whenever the shop is operating. The 14 days are my estimate for finishing the lessons and getting an exam date; the classroom version costs $114 (from research notes). The certificate does not expire.

setup.name: Batch brewer, bulk grinder and airpots
setup.note: Research notes: Bunn CWTF15-APS brewer $980 (KaTom, 2026; the page refused my request) + $800 allowance for a bulk grinder and airpots. Drip coffee is the fastest thing on the menu at the morning peak.

setup.name: Second grinder for decaf
setup.note: A second Mahlkonig E65S at the same $2,099 seen at Visions Espresso.

setup.name: Ice machine
setup.note: Research notes allowance next to a clearance Manitowoc UYF0140A at $3,479.40; the 2026 list price of the current model is $6,392. Without it you buy bagged ice for iced drinks.

setup.name: Under-counter commercial dishwasher
setup.note: Noble Warewashing HT-UC24 high-temperature under-counter dishwasher with booster heater: $4,449.00 at WebstaurantStore. Not mandatory: washing by hand in the three-compartment sink (wash, rinse, sanitize) is legal.

setup.name: Menu boards, lighting and decor
setup.note: Research notes allowance for movable furniture, menus, lighting and decor; fixed counters are in the build-out.

setup.name: Storefront sign
setup.note: Research notes, "almost ready" column: design, fabrication and installation, quote-only. Seen at the Department of Buildings: a wall sign of six square feet or less needs no sign permit; bigger signs need a permit obtained by a licensed sign hanger.

setup.name: Upgrade to a three-group espresso machine
setup.note: Nuova Simonelli Appia Life three-group volumetric, 220V: $11,700.00 at WebstaurantStore; the upgrade costs the difference from the $7,600 compact two-group = $4,100. Needs a 220V line. The quality bonus is a game value.

setup.name: Shop grinder for filter coffee and retail bags
setup.note: Mahlkonig EK43: $3,899 at Visions Espresso. The quality bonus is a game value.

setup.name: Customer restroom upgrade (needed for 20 or more seats)
setup.note: My allowance for bringing an existing staff toilet up to an accessible customer restroom; quote-only, not in the research notes. Seen at NYC Health: a restaurant with 20 or more seats, indoor and outdoor together, must have a customer bathroom.

setup.name: Dining Out NYC sidewalk cafe license
setup.agency: NYC Department of Transportation (Dining Out NYC)
setup.note: Dining Out NYC fees: $1,050 license for a four-year term + $1,500 refundable security deposit for a sidewalk cafe = $2,550; on top comes a yearly consent fee of $6, $10, $18 or $31 per sq ft by sector. The 240-day wait is the Transportation Department's own eight-month estimate; the Comptroller found in October 2026 that more than half of approved restaurants waited over 19 months. Never part of a starter kit.

kits.name: Lean start
kits.pitch: The legal minimum in a small room: 12 seats, one grinder, hand-washed cups, no sign. Cheapest way to open, but the room fills up at 170 orders a day.

kits.name: Standard
kits.pitch: The usual neighborhood cafe: 18 seats, drip coffee and iced drinks, a proper sign. Sized for 200 orders a day with room to spare.

kits.name: Premium
kits.pitch: 24 seats, a three-group machine, top grinders, a dishwasher and a customer restroom (required from 20 seats). Higher quality, about $29,000 more up front, and more seats to fill.

monthlyCosts.name: Rent
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: $90 per sq ft a year x 800 sq ft / 12 = $6,000, a moderate Brooklyn side street (REBNY 2025: small Park Slope spaces ask under $100). The game takes rent from the place on the map; this line is the fallback. See extra.rentByTier.

monthlyCosts.name: Electricity, gas, water and sewer
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: planning band $800-$1,800. Electricity alone at 3,000-5,000 kWh x 23.1 cents (NYSERDA statewide commercial average, August 2026) is $693-$1,155. The kWh figure is the notes' assumption.

monthlyCosts.name: Business owner's policy: liability, property, interruption
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: NYC reserve of $150-$400, base $250. Seen at Insureon: coffee shops pay $126 a month on average across the US for a business owner's policy. Workers' compensation is separate (in _common taxes).

monthlyCosts.name: Cups, lids, sleeves, napkins, bags
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: 2% of sales = $0.17 per $8.50 order. Seen at WebstaurantStore: a 12 oz hot cup is 4.6 cents ($45.99 per 1,000); lid, sleeve, napkin and bag come on top.

monthlyCosts.name: Card processing: percentage fee
monthlyCosts.note: Seen in Square's fee table: 2.5% + 15 cents per tap on the Plus plan (2.6% on Free). Research notes model: 90% of sales on cards, and the percentage is charged on sales tax and tips too: 0.9 x 2.5% x 1.08875 + 2.5% x $2,000 of card tips / $51,000 of sales = 2.55% of sales.

monthlyCosts.name: Card processing: 15 cents per tap
monthlyCosts.note: 15 cents per card transaction (seen in Square's fee table) x 90% of orders paid by card = 13.5 cents per order. With the percentage fee the total is about 4.1% of sales on an $8.50 ticket.

monthlyCosts.name: Employer payroll tax on reported tips
monthlyCosts.note: Tips are wages for payroll tax (IRS Publication 15). Research notes assume $2,000 of card tips a month on $51,000 of sales: 7.65% x $2,000 = $153 = 0.3% of sales.

monthlyCosts.name: Paid sick leave cover
monthlyCosts.note: Up to 40 paid hours a year per worker for employers with 5-99 workers (seen at DCWP): 40 h x $21 / 12 = $70 a month per worker when it is all used.

monthlyCosts.name: Equipment service, filters, grease interceptor, fire extinguisher checks
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: band $200-$500: filter cartridges, descaling and calibration, the yearly backflow test and extinguisher service, grease interceptor cleaning, replacing smallwares.

monthlyCosts.name: Private carter: trash, recycling, organics
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: band $150-$400; not a city rate. Seen at the Sanitation Department: businesses sign with one of three carters authorized for their commercial waste zone, and each carter has a maximum price that depends on volume.

monthlyCosts.name: Internet and phone
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: band $80-$150; Verizon business internet starts at $69 a month plus fees.

monthlyCosts.name: POS software subscription
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: Square Plus $49 per location a month (Free plan $0, Premium $149). The plan prices were not readable on the page when I opened it.

monthlyCosts.name: Bookkeeping and year-end accountant
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes allowance, band $300-$800; no reliable public NYC price. Not a quote.

monthlyCosts.name: Payroll service
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: Gusto Simple $49 a month + $6 per person, five people = $79, rounded up. Files the payroll tax returns for you.

monthlyCosts.name: Website, listings, menus and printing
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: chosen budget inside a $100-$600 band, not an industry norm.

monthlyCosts.name: Permit renewals and filing fees
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: $30-$100 a month set aside. Seen: the Food Service Establishment Permit renews at $280 a year ($23 a month); the rest covers the $25 state LLC fee, scale and sign fees.

staff.name: Barista
staff.note: Research notes planning wage: $21 an hour, above the New York City minimum of $17.00 (seen at NY DOL; it stays $17.00 in 2027). Baristas keep their tips on top. This pack takes no tip credit, so the cash wage equals the full wage: the tipped rate of $11.35 + $5.65 credit is legal only with written notice and tips that cover the gap (12 NYCRR 146-1.3).

staff.name: Shift lead
staff.licenseRequired: NYC Food Protection Certificate (free online course, $24 exam)
staff.note: My estimate: a $3 premium over the barista wage for opening, closing and cash-out. A shift lead with a Food Protection Certificate covers the rule that a certified supervisor is on site every open hour.

taxes.name: NYC sales tax on food and drinks
taxes.appliesIf: coffee and tea served in a cup, food eaten in the shop, heated food and sandwiches
taxes.note: NYC Department of Finance: 4.5% city + 4% state + 0.375% Metropolitan Commuter Transportation District = 8.875%; food and beverages sold by restaurants are taxable. Charged on top of the menu price and held for the state. Bags of beans to take home and some unheated bakery items sold to go are exempt (NYS tax bulletins, from research notes); the game taxes every order, as the notes' model does.

options.label: Staff clean every day, deep clean once a month
House blend from a wholesale roaster

shortcuts.name: Run shifts with no certified supervisor
shortcuts.what: A Food Protection Certificate holder must be on site every hour you are open. Covering every shift means training more people and paying leads; skipping it saves about $120 a month. Each inspection that finds nobody certified costs $400 and 10 points.

shortcuts.name: Sell yesterday's milk and pastries
shortcuts.what: Nothing gets thrown out: old pastries go back in the case, milk sits on the counter. Saves about 1% of sales in waste. Spoiled or warm food is a public health hazard: $250-$600 per citation and a fast road to a C grade.

shortcuts.name: Sell pastries baked at home
shortcuts.what: Baking at home instead of buying from a licensed bakery cuts pastry cost by more than half, about 3% of sales. Food from a home kitchen is food from an unapproved source: $400-$600 and a public health hazard on your record.

shortcuts.name: Keep part of the tips
shortcuts.what: The owner takes a cut of the tip jar and the card tips: about $150 per barista a month. Tips belong to the staff by law. A wage claim returns every dollar double and reaches back six years.

shortcuts.name: Unpaid trial shifts and training
shortcuts.what: New hires work a few shifts "on trial" and train for free: about $85 per worker a month. Every hour worked must be paid at $17.00 or more; unpaid hours are owed back double.

shortcuts.name: Long days without the extra hour
shortcuts.what: Open-to-close and split shifts stretch a workday past 10 hours. The law adds one extra hour of pay at $17.00 for each such day; skipping it saves about $135 per worker a month and is owed back double.

shortcuts.name: Put tables on the sidewalk without a license
shortcuts.what: A few tables outside bring about 2% more sales, and you skip the $1,050 license, the $1,500 deposit and a wait that often runs past a year. The city fines $500, then $1,000 each time, and can order the tables removed.

shortcuts.name: Skip grease interceptor cleaning
shortcuts.what: Milk fat and coffee grounds fill the grease interceptor under the sink. Skipping the pump-out saves about $75 a month. Inspectors measure it: more than 25% full means a fine of $100 to $1,500, and a backup floods your floor.

violations.name: Operating without a Food Service Establishment Permit
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.05(a); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 18-01
violations.note: Penalty schedule: "No current valid permit, registration, other authorization to operate establishment" $1,000, or $2,000 if you do not answer the summons. The Department can order an unpermitted establishment closed; the 5 closure days are my estimate. Opening on the 22nd day after applying is legal even without a pre-permit inspection (NYC Business).

violations.name: No Food Protection Certificate holder on site
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.15(a); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 04A
violations.note: Penalty schedule: "Food Protection Certificate not held by supervisor or manager of food operations" $400; scoring worksheet: 10 points, a critical violation. A certificate that exists but cannot be shown costs $200 (code 18-11). The NYC Business restaurant page quotes $500-$1,000 for the same violation; I use the penalty schedule.

violations.name: Food contact surfaces not washed, rinsed and sanitized
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.27(b), §81.17(e); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, codes 06D and 10F
violations.note: Penalty schedule: code 06D $200 to $300 by condition level (a critical violation, 5 to 8 points); dirty floors, walls and ceilings (code 10F) $100, or $0 the first time if you prove you fixed it. Game formula climbs from $225 to the $300 top as months pass. Fines are small; the points that cost you the A grade are the real price.

violations.name: Mice, rats or roaches; no pest control contract
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.23(a), §81.23(b)(2); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, codes 04K, 04L, 04M and 28-06
violations.note: Penalty schedule: rats, mice or live roaches $200 to $350 by condition level, plus $100 when the contract with a pest management professional and the service records are not on the premises. Scoring worksheet: 5 to 8 points, 28 at the worst level, which alone means a C. Game formula: $350 in the first month up to $450. The Health Code requires a contract with monthly visits by a state-licensed exterminator (from research notes, §81.23(b)). The 2 closure days are my estimate for an infestation that cannot be fixed during the inspection.

violations.name: Spoiled food or cold food kept above 41°F
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.07(a), §81.09(a); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, codes 04H and 02G
violations.note: Penalty schedule: "Cold TCS food not held at 41°F or below" $250 to $500; "Food not protected from adulteration or contamination" $250 to $600. Both are public health hazards that must be corrected immediately. Scoring worksheet: 7 to 10 points, 28 at the worst level. Game formula: $300 in the first month, up to $600.

violations.name: Food from an unapproved source or a home kitchen
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.04; 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 03A
violations.note: Penalty schedule: "Food from unapproved or unknown source, or home cooked" $400 to $600, a public health hazard worth 10 points, 28 at the worst level. Game formula: $450 in the first month, up to $600.

violations.name: Owner keeping workers' tips
violations.note: Labor Law §196-d: no employer or agent may demand, accept or keep any part of the gratuities received by an employee. §198(1-a): the amount owed plus liquidated damages of 100%, interest and attorney's fees, with a six-year reach. §218: a civil penalty of up to double for willful or repeat cases. Game formula: 2.0 x what was kept.

violations.name: Unpaid trial shifts and training time
violations.note: Every hour worked is owed at the minimum wage or more ($17.00 in New York City, 12 NYCRR 146); a worker who reports for a shift is owed at least three hours of pay (12 NYCRR §146-1.5). Labor Law §198(1-a): the unpaid wages plus 100% liquidated damages and interest. Game formula: 2.0 x what was withheld.

violations.name: Spread-of-hours pay not paid
violations.note: 12 NYCRR §146-1.6: on each day on which the spread of hours exceeds 10, an employee shall receive one additional hour of pay at the basic minimum hourly rate; it applies to all restaurant employees whatever their pay rate. Owed back with 100% liquidated damages (Labor Law §198). Game formula: 2.0 x what was withheld.

violations.name: Sidewalk tables without a Dining Out NYC license
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §19-160 and following (Dining Out NYC, Local Law 121 of 2023)
violations.note: Dining Out NYC enforcement page: unlicensed setups get a penalty with no warning: $500 for the first offense, $1,000 for the second and later offenses, and the Transportation Department may order the setup removed. The game charges $500 per citation. Section and local law numbers are cited from memory.

violations.name: Grease interceptor not maintained
violations.law: 15 RCNY §19-11 (NYC Department of Environmental Protection sewer use rules)
violations.note: NYC Business restaurant page: grease interceptors must be properly sized, installed and maintained; fats, oils and grease must not exceed 25% of the liquid depth or rated capacity; fine $100 to $1,500. The rule covers coffee shops and drains that receive dairy (from research notes, 15 RCNY §19-11). Game formula spreads the range over time: $300 after one month, $1,500 from the seventh.

officials.name: Health inspector
officials.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
officials.realProcess: Unannounced, at least once a year. The inspector walks the whole shop with a thermometer and a flashlight and scores each violation in points: under 14 is an A. With 14 or more, a second inspection comes at least 7 days later and sets the grade. Fines are decided afterwards at a city hearing (OATH).

officials.name: Outdoor dining inspector
officials.agency: NYC Department of Transportation (Dining Out NYC)
officials.realProcess: Inspectors patrol and answer 311 complaints. A licensed cafe with a setup problem gets 30 days to correct it; an unlicensed one is fined at once and can be ordered to clear the sidewalk.

officials.name: Sewer inspector
officials.realProcess: Inspectors visit food businesses, open the grease interceptor, measure how full it is and ask for cleaning records.

reports.name: Report unsanitary conditions (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint about a food establishment. The Health Department sends an inspector unannounced; pests, dirty equipment, spoiled or home-made food all count. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report operating without a permit (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to the Health Department. An inspector checks the permit on the wall and asks who on the shift holds a Food Protection Certificate. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report unlicensed sidewalk tables or grease dumping (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint routed to the Transportation Department (outdoor dining) or Environmental Protection (grease in the sewer). An inspector checks the license and the grease interceptor. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report wage or tip theft (NYS Department of Labor)
reports.text: In real life: a labor standards complaint, which a worker or anyone else can file. An investigator audits time records, pay stubs and the tip log. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

events.name: Wholesale coffee up 20%
events.text: Roasters pass on higher green coffee prices. Beans are about a quarter of what an order costs you to make.
events.note: Seen at FRED (BLS average price, ground roast coffee, US city average): $9.25 per lb in October 2026, $9.46 in June 2026. The 20% rise and the bean share of cost of goods (about 25%) are my estimates: 20% x 25% = +5% on cost of goods.

events.name: Milk up 10%
events.text: Your dairy distributor raises prices. Milk goes into most of the drinks you sell.
events.note: Seen at FRED (BLS average price, whole milk, US city average): $4.10 per gallon in October 2026, $4.32 in June 2026: a 5% swing in four months. The 10% rise and the dairy share of cost of goods (about 30%) are my estimates.

events.name: NYC Restaurant Week
events.text: Prix-fixe menus at $30, $45 and $60 pull diners into the neighborhood. More people walk past your door.
events.note: Seen at NYC Tourism: Restaurant Week Winter 2027 runs January 19 to February 11 with menus at $30, $45 and $60 at hundreds of restaurants. The 5% lift for a coffee shop is my estimate.

events.name: Sidewalk shed goes up on your block
events.text: Scaffolding covers your storefront while the building next door repairs its facade. Fewer people notice the shop.
events.note: Seen at the Department of Buildings: sidewalk sheds protect pedestrians during construction or facade work; a first permit is generally valid for a year. The 10% drop is my estimate.

events.name: Summer electricity peak
events.text: Air conditioning, ice machine and fridges run flat out while electricity is at its yearly high.
events.note: Research notes, NYSERDA statewide commercial average price: 22.3 cents per kWh in January 2026, 24.2 cents in July 2026: 8.5% higher. The page refused my request, so the figures are from the notes.

events.name: Flu season
events.text: Half the team is sick in the same fortnight. Sick workers are entitled to paid leave, and the bar runs short-handed.
events.note: Seen at DCWP: employers with 99 or fewer workers owe up to 40 hours of paid protected time off a year. The 8% loss of working hours is my estimate.

ruleCards.title: Letter grades
ruleCards.text: Every NYC cafe is inspected unannounced at least once a year. 0-13 points is an A, 14-27 a B, 28 or more a C, and the card must hang where passersby can see it. Not posting it costs $500; tampering with it costs $1,000.

ruleCards.title: Food Service Establishment Permit
ruleCards.text: A cafe needs a Food Service Establishment Permit from the Health Department: $280 a year. You may open on the 22nd day after applying even if no inspector has come yet; the first inspection then arrives unannounced.

ruleCards.title: No permit
ruleCards.text: Serving food or drinks without a current Health Department permit costs $1,000 ($2,000 if you ignore the summons), and the Department can order the shop closed until the permit is issued.

ruleCards.title: Food Protection Certificate
ruleCards.text: A supervisor with a Food Protection Certificate must be on site every hour you are open. The online course is free and the exam costs $24. Nobody certified at inspection: $400 and 10 points, most of the way to losing your A.

ruleCards.title: Clean, rinse, sanitize
ruleCards.text: Surfaces that touch food must be washed, rinsed and sanitized. A dirty steam wand, grinder or cutting board is a critical violation: $200-$300 and 5 to 8 points each time. Dirty floors and walls add $100 and 2 to 5 points.

ruleCards.title: Pests
ruleCards.text: Mice, rats or roaches cost $200-$350 per citation and 5 to 28 points: at the worst level that alone is a C. The Health Code also requires a contract with a licensed exterminator kept on site ($100 if it is missing).

ruleCards.title: Cold food and old food
ruleCards.text: Cold food must stay at 41°F or below. Milk left on the counter or spoiled food kept for sale is a public health hazard: $250-$600 per citation, and the shop can be closed if it is not fixed on the spot.

ruleCards.title: Where your food comes from
ruleCards.text: Everything you sell must come from a licensed source. Pastries baked in a home kitchen count as food from an unapproved source: a public health hazard, $400-$600, however good they taste.

ruleCards.title: Tips belong to the staff
ruleCards.text: Tips belong to the workers. An owner or manager may not keep any part of them (NY Labor Law §196-d). Taken tips are owed back with 100% damages and interest, and claims reach back six years.

ruleCards.title: Trial shifts are paid
ruleCards.text: Trial shifts, training and staff meetings are work. Each hour must be paid at $17.00 or more, and anyone who reports for a shift is owed at least 3 hours of pay. Unpaid hours are owed back double.

ruleCards.title: Spread of hours
ruleCards.text: If a workday stretches over more than 10 hours from start to finish, breaks and split shifts included, the worker is owed one extra hour at the minimum wage: $17.00 in New York City.

ruleCards.title: Sidewalk tables
ruleCards.text: Tables on the sidewalk need a Dining Out NYC license: $1,050 for four years, a $1,500 deposit and a yearly fee of $6-$31 per square foot. Without it: $500 for the first offense, $1,000 for each one after, and the city can remove the setup.

ruleCards.title: Outdoor dining takes a long time
ruleCards.text: Plan the first year without outdoor seats. The city Comptroller found in 2026 that more than half of the restaurants approved for outdoor dining had waited over 19 months for the permit.

ruleCards.title: Grease interceptor
ruleCards.text: Coffee shops need a grease interceptor too: milk fat counts. It must be properly sized and installed, and cleaned before grease fills 25% of it. Fines run from $100 to $1,500.

ruleCards.title: The 20-seat line
ruleCards.text: With 20 or more seats, counting outdoor ones, a cafe must give customers a bathroom. Under 20 seats you do not need a customer bathroom, but you still need a hand-washing sink near the bar and in every restroom.

ruleCards.title: Tipped wage
ruleCards.text: A tipped food service worker in NYC may be paid $11.35 in cash plus a $5.65 tip credit only with written notice, records, and tips that really cover the gap. Otherwise the full $17.00 is due. The safe choice is to pay the full wage.

ruleCards.title: What is taxed in a cafe
ruleCards.text: Coffee in a cup is taxed at 8.875% even to go. Food eaten in the shop, heated food and sandwiches are taxed too. Bags of beans to take home are not. Set the register up item by item: the tax you collect is never part of your sales.

ruleCards.title: Card fees on small tickets
ruleCards.text: Card fees are not just 2.5%. With 15 cents per tap, and the fee charged on tax and tips too, an $8.50 order costs about 35 cents to process: around 4% of sales. Small tickets pay the highest share.

ruleCards.title: After a bad inspection
ruleCards.text: Score 14 or more on the first inspection and the inspector returns no sooner than 7 days later to set your grade. A B brings the next cycle in 5-7 months, a C in 3-5 months, instead of once a year.

ruleCards.title: Storefront signs
ruleCards.text: A wall sign of 6 square feet or less needs no Buildings Department sign permit. Anything bigger needs a permit that only a licensed sign hanger can obtain. Read the lease as well: the landlord usually has to approve the sign.

ruleCards.title: Business trash
ruleCards.text: The city does not collect business trash. You must sign with a private carter authorized for your commercial waste zone (three per zone) and post its decal. Each carter has a maximum price that depends on how much you put out.

ruleCards.title: Fair Workweek
ruleCards.text: New York City's Fair Workweek Law covers fast food chains with 30 or more locations nationwide: schedules 14 days ahead and premiums for changes. One independent cafe is not covered, but call-in pay and spread-of-hours rules still apply.

ruleCards.title: Take over a former cafe
ruleCards.text: A space that was already a cafe saves the most money. Building a counter-service cafe in a former food space costs $200-$300 per square foot in NYC; a space that never had food service can run $400-$600 or more.

benchmarks.note: Seen at the National Restaurant Association (2025 release, 2024 data, more than 900 US restaurants): limited-service operators had a median pre-tax income of 4.0% of sales and prime costs (food, drinks and labor) of 65%. Cost of goods 28% is the research notes' model; labor 35% is the rest of the 65% prime cost, rounded; rent 10% is my New York planning ceiling: the national median for city-center limited service is 6.0% (NRA, from research notes), while the notes' Brooklyn model runs 11.8%.

roadmap.title: Decide the format: counter service, menu, seats
roadmap.text: Coffee and bought-in pastries with no cooking keeps you out of hoods, fire suppression and gas permits. Stay under 20 seats and you do not have to build a customer bathroom. Count people walking past your target corner at 8am before you count on 200 orders a day.

roadmap.title: Scout storefronts: look for a former cafe
roadmap.text: About 800 sq ft holds 18-24 seats. A former cafe keeps its plumbing, ventilation and bathroom: a light renovation runs near $90 per sq ft instead of $200-$300. Typical asking rents for 800 sq ft: about $3,000 a month in outer Queens, $6,000 on a Brooklyn side street, $22,000 in prime Manhattan.

roadmap.title: Check the Certificate of Occupancy before you sign
roadmap.text: The building's Certificate of Occupancy must allow an eating and drinking place; buildings from before 1938 may need a Letter of No Objection instead. Also check electrical capacity, the grease interceptor, an accessible restroom and whether the block is landmarked. Make the lease depend on getting your permits.

roadmap.title: Design and build out
roadmap.text: An architect files plans, licensed plumbers and electricians pull the permits. Budget $70,000 for a light renovation of a former cafe plus about 10% for drawings and filings. Expect 6-14 weeks for permits and 8-24 weeks of construction, with rent due once any free-rent period ends.

roadmap.title: Pass the Food Protection Course
roadmap.text: Take the free 15-lesson online course and pay $24 for the in-person exam. A certified supervisor must be in the shop every hour it is open, so certify yourself and at least one more person. You need the certificate or a course registration to apply for the permit.

roadmap.title: Get your Food Service Establishment Permit
roadmap.text: Apply online with proof of workers' compensation and disability insurance, the sales tax Certificate of Authority and the Food Protection Certificate. The fee is $280 a year. You may open on the 22nd day after applying; call for a pre-operational inspection if you want to open sooner.
roadmap.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)

roadmap.title: Grease interceptor and private carter
roadmap.text: Have a licensed plumber confirm the grease interceptor is the right size. Sign a contract with one of the three private carters authorized for your commercial waste zone and post the decal: the city does not pick up business trash.
roadmap.agency: NYC Department of Environmental Protection; NYC Department of Sanitation

roadmap.title: Check the sign rules before you order a sign
roadmap.text: A wall sign of 6 sq ft or less needs no sign permit. A bigger or illuminated sign must be filed with the Department of Buildings and hung by a licensed sign hanger, and the landlord usually has to approve it.

roadmap.title: Optional: apply for sidewalk seating
roadmap.text: Sidewalk tables need a Dining Out NYC license: $1,050 for four years plus a $1,500 refundable deposit and a yearly fee per square foot. Apply early, but plan year one without outdoor seats: more than half of approved restaurants waited over 19 months.
roadmap.agency: NYC Department of Transportation (Dining Out NYC)

roadmap.title: Buy equipment and furniture
roadmap.text: A new basic set costs about $36,500 before tax and delivery: espresso machine $7,600, two grinders $4,200, fridges and pastry case $3,800, sinks, ice machine, dishwasher, register, 20 chairs and 10 tables. Order the machine first: delivery takes 2-4 weeks. Used gear from a closing cafe cuts the bill.

roadmap.title: Line up suppliers and the opening order
roadmap.text: Pick a wholesale roaster (many train your staff and service the machine), a dairy distributor, a wholesale bakery that delivers before 7am, and a source for cups and lids. Open accounts two to three weeks ahead; the first order runs $3,000-$5,000.

roadmap.title: Set up the register and card payments
roadmap.text: A Square register costs about $900; processing is 2.5%-2.6% plus 15 cents per tap. Program each menu item as taxable or not, switch on tip reporting, and connect payroll so tips and hours flow into pay stubs.

roadmap.title: Hire and train baristas
roadmap.text: Four baristas cover a 12-hour day at 200 orders. Minimum wage is $17.00; the model pays $21 plus tips. Pay for training and trial shifts, give each hire a written pay notice, and schedule to avoid overtime and days longer than 10 hours.

roadmap.title: Open your doors
roadmap.text: Open once the permit is in hand or on the 22nd day after applying. Post the permit, keep the Food Protection Certificate and the pest control contract in the shop, and expect an unannounced first inspection. Keep three months of fixed costs in the bank: the first months are slower than the plan.

manager.note: Research notes: the economic price of a manager who replaces the owner, 160 hours x $30 = $4,800 a month before employer payroll taxes. A planning figure, not a wage statistic.

realTimeline.note: The game waits only for the two Health Department items (21 days). In real life the build-out sets the date: permit path 6-14 weeks, long-lead equipment 8-20 weeks, construction 8-24 weeks, inspections 1-3 weeks (contractor's 2026 estimates, steps overlap). The research notes budget three paid months of rent before opening for a former cafe and six for a heavy conversion.

footfall.note: Demand = people walking the block a day (data/places.json, modelled from MTA station entries and DOHMH food places and scaled to DOT sidewalk counts: data/open/fit.json) x the share who buy here. captureRate is that share for a known, average shop with no rival in sight at the reference price; real coffee shops within 250 m (DOHMH) and playing shops split the same people, and 'outside' is everyone who buys coffee somewhere else or not at all. No public statistic of cafe conversion exists. The rate, the price sensitivity and the ramp were set on the bench against three targets: an established shop on a sound block clears a few thousand dollars a month at about $9 an order, the best price sits within 10% of the reference price at doors where the room is not full, and about one newcomer in five who follows the recommended plan closes in the first year (the game's target, build/ROUND3.md B11; not a measured rate). A new shop starts at half of its regular crowd (opening-week curiosity; most affordable rooms are former cafes whose block already buys coffee at that door) and closes about two thirds of the gap every 60 days. Bench, 14 Nov 2026 (agents/r3-B11.md): with 0.088 / 0.35 / 75 days, 13 of 18 newcomer cafes closed in four simulated seasons (npx tsx sim/trace.ts 2 --no-runway, seeds 100 and 200); with 0.095 / 0.5 / 60 days, 6 of 18, three of them before the doors opened because the plan left less cash than the rent of the wait. Every one of these is an estimate waiting for evidence: research/prompts/80-codex-real-factors.md, part A.

buildout.note: Cost per sq ft: research notes (economics.md), three columns of the 2026 opening budget. Days: the notes count 3, 3 and 6 months of paid rent before the first sale; the contractor's 2026 guide gives 8-24 weeks of construction after 6-14 weeks of permits, overlapping (contractor estimates, not official deadlines). Here the light job takes 60 days, the standard one 90 and the heavy one 180, and the Health Department permit adds its wait after the room is finished. Rent is due from the day the lease is signed.

takeover.note: Buying an operating coffee shop: the price covers the finished room, the equipment and the furniture, and nine in ten regulars stay. The research notes list key money as quote-only with no public figure; the asking price here is 20% of a year of sales the address supports at the reference price, between $80,000 and $200,000 - a planning rule of thumb, not a listing. The buyer still signs a lease (new deposit), applies for a new Health Department permit (it does not transfer), restocks and hires. Estimate waiting for evidence: research/prompts/80-codex-real-factors.md, part A.
